content_list.content_text: The virgins played with passion by Lillian Gish and with humor by Mary Pickford during the silent era were countered by two comparatively short-lived manifestations of the sexualized woman. In the mid-1910s came the vamp, the voracious upper-class man-eater, iconically portrayed by Theda Bara in A Fool There Was (1915). In the 1920s, the vamp gave way to the flapper, a hedonistic but not at all malicious figure, most successfully embodied by Colleen Moore and Clara Bow, the It Girl.

Virgins and vamps hark back to Victorian melodrama and were fantasies rooted in idealized and demonized notions of femininity. Having arrived after World War I, the flapper was one facet of the new emancipated woman, who worked, voted, smoked, drank, danced to jazz and had sex. The other facet was the sophisticated wife, played with great daring by Gloria Swanson (1899-1983) and her extravagant outfits in six bedroom comedies by Cecil B. DeMille (1881-1959). The sexy working girl and the liberated wife merged into one, giving rise to the sharp-tongued modern woman of the screwball comedy, or madcap comedy, of the 1930s, a subgenre that can be considered the forerunner of the romantic comedy.

information.contentTitle: The only surviving scenes from Cleopatra
information.contentText: Theda Bara in a revealing costume typical of her, as the Egyptian queen in Cleopatra, directed by J. Gordon Edwards (1867-1925). A phenomenon of early cinema, her exotic and mysterious image was created and promoted by Fox.

content_list.content_text: Just as the femme fatale of 1940s film noir was a product of male anxieties during a period of national instability, the vamp was a sociological construct. Unlike the femme fatale, however, she would not later be redeemed by feminist scholars. She emerged as a celluloid phantom, drawn from Sir Philip Burne-Jones's painting The Vampire, from the poem of the same name by his cousin Rudyard Kipling and from the novel Dracula by Bram Stoker, all from 1897. Kipling's poem inspired the Broadway play A Fool There Was, a 1909 hit directed by Porter Emerson Browne and adapted for the screen in 1915.

Bara explored her vampish traits in a series of seductive characters, her eyes painted black, most recognizably in Cleopatra (1917). However, Bara was not American cinema's first vampire. Alice Hollister preceded her in The Vampire (1913), in which vaudeville dancers Alice Eis and Bert French re-created their "Vampire Dance," which had been a stage hit in 1909. As a supernatural woman who sucks the life force out of a lawyer, Bara became the most sensual of all the femme fatales.

content_list.title: From the Page to the Screen
content_list.description:
Theda Bara was neither the first nor the last star to have her name changed by the Hollywood studios. Florence Lawrence, "The Biograph Girl," considered the "first movie star," who in 1910 also became the first actress to have her real name in the credits, was actually Florence Annie Bridgwood.

Many other stars were given — or chose, though this was rarer — stage names. Sometimes it was a matter of euphony: Julius Ulman became Douglas Fairbanks, while Frances Gumm metamorphosed into Judy Garland . Some names carried unfortunate associations: Hedwig Kiesler's surname was considered too similar to keister (slang for "rear end"), and so she became Hedy Lamarr.

Only when the power of the old studios began to wane were actors like Jack Lemmon able to refuse to be renamed. More recently, stars such as Arnold Schwarzenegger and Renée Zellweger have built extraordinary careers while proudly keeping their surnames.
content_list.credits: Summary based on the text by Dominic Power, published in the book "Cinema: The Whole Story" by Philip Kemp

content_list.content_text: In 1920, F. Scott Fitzgerald symbolically ushered in the Roaring Twenties with This Side of Paradise, his sensational debut novel, and Olive Thomas, who had originated the "baby vamp " in Upstairs and Down (1919), played a schoolgirl pretending to be a jazz girl in The Flapper — the first time the term was used in the United States. Fitzgerald claimed that Colleen Moore was the quintessential flapper for her performance in Flaming Youth (1923).

Moore became a box-office phenomenon, though she was more spirited than seductive. The same could not be said of Bow in films such as It (1927), in which she shone as a department store salesgirl set on landing her boss. Screenwriter Elinor Glyn even makes an appearance in the film to explain the meaning of "it," a euphemism for the character's sex appeal.
content_list.content_credits: Summary based on the text by Graham Fuller, published in the book "Cinema: The Whole Story" by Philip Kemp

content_list.content_text: Alice Guy Blaché had been hired as a secretary at the Comptoir Général de Photographie, which would be acquired the following year by Léon Gaumont. Under the Gaumont name, the world's first film company was born — and the oldest still in operation. Despite the change at the company, the young woman, then in her twenties, kept working as a secretary — but she would not stay in the job for long.

information.contentText: In an interview given back in 1912, the director caused a stir by telling the newspapers that women were already prepared to vote — something that would only become a reality in the country in 1920.

content_list.content_text: Together with the Gaumont team, Alice Guy was invited to witness the magic of the first cinematograph developed by the Lumière brothers. The device, revolutionary for its time, worked as both camera and projector. As she watched the scenes of La Sortie de l’usine Lumière à Lyon (Workers Leaving the Lumière Factory, 1895), she foresaw the potential of the new technology. The daughter of a bookseller, Alice had always been used to reading and had even done some theater for a while. Her familiarity with storytelling led her to look at cinema in a new way. She decided to turn it into a vehicle for telling stories.
And so, in 1896, Alice released the world's first non-fiction film. La Fée aux choux (The Cabbage Fairy, 1896), just one minute long, was written, produced and directed by her.

Although the Lumière brothers made a short scene titled L’Arroseur arrosé (The Sprinkler Sprinkled, 1895) in 1895, they had no inkling of cinema's full potential and saw it more as a tool for recording than as a way of telling stories. In contrast, Alice Guy's first film features sets, cuts, special effects and a narrative, however brief. It is based on an old French legend according to which baby boys are born from cabbages, while girls are born from roses.

information.contentText: Most of her subsequent films were biblical epics, and she created one of the world's first film studios, Solax, in New York State, where she had emigrated in 1907. In all, she is believed to have directed around seven hundred short films, including Westerns and thrillers.

content_list.content_text: Alice herself remade the production twice, releasing new versions in 1900 and 1902. Of the 1900 film, a fragment kept by the Svenska Filminstitutet, the Swedish Film Institute, was recovered.

According to her granddaughter Adrienne Blaché-Channing in The Lost Garden: The Life and Cinema of Alice Guy-Blaché (1995), Alice's first commercial film sold 80 copies, a success for its time. Its strong reception led the young woman to be quickly promoted to head of film production at Gaumont. Quite a position for a woman in the 19th century.

By ushering in a new era of cinema, in which filming was no longer restricted to depicting reality, she could not have been more deserving of the role. From that moment on, the creators' imagination was the only limit for the Seventh Art. That same year, Georges Méliès would release his first film. He became famous; Alice was nearly forgotten by history.

quote.quote: There is nothing connected with the making of a film that a woman cannot do as easily as a man, being fully capable of mastering every technical detail of this art.
quote.author: Alice Guy Blaché

content_list.content_text: The greatest success of her career came the same year, when Alice released La Vie du Christ (The Birth, the Life and the Death of Christ, 1906), a 34-minute short film that explores film language as never before. With special effects, scene cuts and deep characters, she laid the first foundation upon which the blockbusters of the future would be built. Also in 1906, the director released the film Les résultats du féminisme (The Consequences of Feminism, 1906), which shows men performing activities typically associated with women, while the women enjoy themselves at the bar and harass their partners. In less than 7 minutes, the comedy uses laughter to poke at the status quo.

On a business trip, the director met her colleague Herbert Blaché, whom she married, and was removed from her post at Gaumont – he, of course, kept his job. In 1907, her husband was sent to the United States as the company's production manager. Determined to start a new life in America, they packed their bags. Once in the United States, Alice founded her own company, Solax, in 1910. The first productions were a success, and by 1912 she was the only woman in the country earning more than $25,000 a year. With that success, she built her own studio in Fort Lee for $100,000 – the equivalent of a $3 million investment today.

information.contentTitle: Excerpts from A Fool and His Money
information.contentText: At a time when white actors wore blackface to portray Black people on screen — a practice that continued for a long time — Alice released in 1912 the first film in history with an all-Black cast, titled A Fool and His Money (1912).

content_list.content_text: The director is believed to have worked on more than a thousand film productions, although only 130 of them have been found to date. Over time, many of her films were credited to men, while others bore only the name of the production company. Her work began to be rediscovered in the '80s, after the posthumous publication of her autobiography, written in the late '40s. In the book, Alice lists the films she produced, in the hope of one day receiving due credit for her work and claiming a place that had always been hers: that of a pioneer of cinema.
content_list.content_credits: Summary based on the article Alice Guy Blaché, a pioneira do cinema que a história esqueceu (Alice Guy Blaché, the film pioneer history forgot), by Philip Kemp

movies.title: The Consequences of Feminism
movies.overview: It's a society in which gender roles are switched. Will men stand to be unequal?

movies.title: A Fool There Was
movies.overview: John Schuyler, a happily married lawyer, is appointed diplomat and sent to England; but, due to an unfortunate accident, his wife and child can not come along with him. Then, on the ship, he meets the Vampire, a notorious woman, a relentless gold digger, who lives off men whom seduces and ruins.

movies.title: It
movies.overview: A flapper shopgirl woos her rich boss with animal magnetism, otherwise known as "it."

movies.title: Cleopatra
movies.overview: The story of Cleopatra, the fabulous queen of Egypt, and the epic romances between her and the greatest men of Rome, Julius Caesar and Antony. (IMDb) Only a fragment of this film is known to still exist.

movies.title: Upstairs and Down
movies.overview: Alice Chesterton is described as a "Baby Vamp" by the social set and engaged to boring Tom Carey. She flirts with many of the male guests idling at the Ives' Long Island house party, then encourages Terence O'Keefe, a playboy polo player from Ireland, to rendezvous with her in the city; they are seen together at the "Midnight Frolic". Because of this, Mrs. Ives convinces Alice's newly-arrived sister Betty to look after Alice.

movies.title: Flesh and the Devil
movies.overview: As lifelong best friends Leo and Ulrich return home following completion of their military training, Leo sees stunning Felicitas at the railway station and, mesmerized by her beauty, is smitten. A scandal follows, for which Leo is sent away. Returning home three years later, he discovers that much has changed.

movies.title: Our Dancing Daughters
movies.overview: A flapper sets her hat for a man with a hard-drinking wife.

movies.title: Pandora's Box
movies.overview: Lulu is a young woman so beautiful and alluring that few can resist her siren charms. The men drawn into her web include respectable newspaper publisher Dr. Ludwig Schön, his musical producer son Alwa, circus performer Rodrigo Quast and Lulu's seedy old friend, Schigolch. When Lulu's charms inevitably lead to tragedy, the downward spiral encompasses them all.

movies.title: The Temptress
movies.overview: A seductive woman forsakes her husband and lover to pursue a young engineer.

movies.title: The Cabbage-Patch Fairy
movies.overview: A brief fantasy tale involving a strange fairy who can produce and deliver babies coming out of cabbages.

movies.title: The Birth, the Life and the Death of Christ
movies.overview: The stations of Christ's life are segmented into a series of performative tableaux.
